1.Nf3 Nf6.strategy: Develops a piece and controls e4 and d5 without committing a pawn, so Black keeps every set-up open and sees White's plan first. It also makes 2.e4 pointless, since the pawn is simply lost to ...Nxe4. The cost is that Black must be at home in several different structures.

1.Nf3 d5.strategy: Claims the centre at once and turns 2.e4 into a gambit, since ...dxe4 takes the pawn. Black gets an early stake in the middle, but White keeps the choice between quiet set-ups that leave the d5-pawn alone and a direct challenge to it, and Black must be ready for both.

1.Nf3 c5.strategy: Fights for d4 at once: if White takes the centre with a pawn, Black trades a flank pawn for a centre pawn. It suits a player who already answers 1.e4 with 1...c5, but White decides whether the game becomes a Sicilian or a symmetrical English, so Black must be ready for either.

1.Nf3 e6.strategy: Opens the f8-bishop and prepares ...d5 while keeping the king's knight and the c-pawn uncommitted. Black can still choose between several solid set-ups. The cost is that White picks the type of game, and after ...d5 the c8-bishop stays hemmed in behind the e6-pawn.

1.Nf3 g6.strategy: Prepares ...Bg7 and leaves the centre for later. The fianchettoed bishop presses on White's centre from a distance, and Black counterattacks with pawn breaks in the centre or on the queenside. White can gain space with pawns on e4 and d4, so Black must be ready to hit the centre.

1.Nf3 f5.name: Zukertort Opening: Dutch Variation
1.Nf3 f5.background: 1...f5 is the move of the Dutch Defence (1.d4 f5), which Elias Stein, an Alsatian who settled in The Hague, recommended as the best reply to 1.d4 in his 1789 book Nouvel essai sur le Jeu des échecs.
1.Nf3 f5.strategy: Takes control of e4 and aims for set-ups in which Black fights for the centre from the flank. Sound and established, but sharper and more committal than the quieter main replies, because it weakens the e8–h5 diagonal and the e6-square. White can test it at once with the gambit 2.e4 fxe4 3.Ng5, which attacks the e4-pawn.

1.Nf3 c6.name: Zukertort Opening: Slav Invitation
1.Nf3 c6.strategy: Prepares ...d5 with the pawn supported, aiming at solid Slav or Caro-Kann structures. It is sound but more passive than the main replies, because the c-pawn move does not develop a piece.

1.Nf3 d6.name: Zukertort Opening: Pirc Invitation
1.Nf3 d6.strategy: Keeps the centre flexible and waits for White to commit. Sound, but it gives White a free hand to build a broad pawn centre, while the d6-pawn only watches e5 and c5.

1.Nf3 b6.name: Zukertort Opening: Queenside Fianchetto Variation
1.Nf3 b6.strategy: Prepares the fianchetto ...Bb7, which presses on e4 along the long diagonal. The set-up is sound but slow: White can take the centre at once, and Black has to attack the pawns afterwards.

1.Nf3 Nc6.name: Zukertort Opening: Black Mustang Defence
1.Nf3 Nc6.strategy: Develops a knight and watches e5 and d4, so Black keeps its central pawn breaks open. The knight blocks the c-pawn and commits itself before White shows a plan. Sound enough, but Black gains nothing over the main replies.

1.Nf3 a6.name: Zukertort Opening: St. George Defence
1.Nf3 a6.background: 1...a6 is the move of the St. George Defence against 1.e4, on which the English IM Michael Basman did much of the theoretical work and with which Tony Miles beat the reigning world champion Anatoly Karpov at the 1980 European Team Championship in Skara.
1.Nf3 a6.strategy: Prepares ...b5 and ...Bb7, but spends a tempo on a rim pawn while White takes the centre. Nothing in the position makes the move urgent, so Black falls behind in space and development.

1.Nf3 a5.name: Zukertort Opening: Ware Defence
1.Nf3 a5.strategy: Gains a little space on the queenside but does nothing for the centre or development, and leaves b6 without the a-pawn's protection. White builds a centre and keeps the extra tempo.

1.Nf3 b5.name: Zukertort Opening: Polish Defence
1.Nf3 b5.strategy: Claims queenside space and prepares ...Bb7, but the pawn on b5 needs constant protection and the c6-square is weakened. White gains time against it with e4, which opens the f1-bishop's diagonal to b5, or with a4.

1.Nf3 Na6.strategy: Heads for b4 or c5, but the knight on the rim covers no central square and blocks the a-pawn. White takes space in the centre and keeps the initiative.

1.Nf3 Nh6.strategy: Eyes f5, but the knight on the rim covers no central square, and after 2.d4 the c1-bishop can take it, doubling Black's h-pawns. Black loses time and White gets the centre without a fight.

1.Nf3 f6.name: Zukertort Opening: Arctic Defence
1.Nf3 f6.strategy: Prepares ...e5, but takes the g8-knight's best square and loosens e6 and the e8–h5 diagonal. After 2.e4 e5 3.Nxe5, taking the knight with 3...fxe5? runs into 4.Qh5+ and a decisive attack.

1.Nf3 h6.name: Zukertort Opening: Basman Defence
1.Nf3 h6.strategy: Prepares ...g5 and ...g4 against the knight on f3, but loses a tempo and loosens the kingside. White builds a centre while Black's flank play achieves little.

1.Nf3 h5.strategy: Spends a tempo on a flank pawn and gives up control of g5, where White's knight can settle because ...h6 is no longer possible. It does nothing for the centre or development.

1.Nf3 e5.name: Zukertort Opening: Ross Gambit
1.Nf3 e5.strategy: Walks into 2.Nxe5, which wins the unprotected pawn. After 2...Nc6 3.Nxc6 dxc6 Black has open lines and quick development, but not enough for the pawn.

1.Nf3 g5.name: Zukertort Opening: Herrstrom Gambit
1.Nf3 g5.strategy: Offers the g-pawn for nothing: 2.Nxg5 wins it, and 2...e5, which uncovers the queen's attack on the knight, only drives it back while White keeps the extra pawn and Black's kingside stays weakened.

1.Nf3.name: Zukertort Opening
1.Nf3.background: Named after Johannes Zukertort. Most sources call only 1.Nf3 d5 2.c4 the Réti Opening, the line with which Richard Réti beat the reigning world champion Capablanca at New York 1924. Réti championed the hypermodern school of the 1920s, which controlled the centre from a distance rather than occupying it with pawns.

1.Nf3 d6 2.d4.strategy: Takes the centre at once with the pawn that the f3 knight already supports. Black's ...d6 does not contest d5, so White occupies space without a fight and can build a broad pawn centre that Black must then challenge.

1.Nf3 d6 2.e4.strategy: Occupies the centre with the king's pawn, using the fact that ...d6 gives up the fight for d5. White gains space and open lines for the pieces, but the e4 pawn has no defender yet and must be supported when attacked.

1.Nf3 e5 2.Nxe5.strategy: Takes the pawn that Black has simply offered. The knight stands on an exposed square where it can be harassed, but White only has to be careful with it, and Black's compensation is a quicker development, not anything concrete.

1.Nf3 f6 2.e4.strategy: Takes the centre at once and punishes the self-block: Black's f-pawn leaves the e8-h5 diagonal loose, so the queen can use it for a check once the knight on f3 moves, and ...e5 is hard to play. White gets space and the easier game.

1.Nf3 Na6 2.e4.strategy: Takes the centre at once against the rim knight. The knight on a6 does not fight for the centre and White can build space, so Black has to prove the knight is useful on the edge by hitting the centre from the flanks.

1.Nf3 Nh6 2.d4.strategy: Takes the centre at once. The knight on h6 sits on the rim, eyeing only f5 and g4 and doing nothing for the centre, so White gains space with no challenge to it and Black must catch up in development.

1.Nf3 e5 2.Nxe5 Nc6.strategy: Attacks the knight on e5, which nothing defends, so it must move or be traded. Black has no pawn to show for the gambit, so the plan is to catch up in development and use the open lines.

1.Nf3 e5 2.Nxe5 Nc6 3.Nxc6.strategy: Trades the exposed knight at once and spoils Black's structure: the recapture leaves doubled c-pawns. White stays a pawn up and has a sound game, while Black gets the open d-file and the bishop's diagonal as compensation.

1.Nf3 e5 2.Nxe5 Nc6 3.Nxc6 dxc6.name: Zukertort Opening: The Walrus
1.Nf3 e5 2.Nxe5 Nc6 3.Nxc6 dxc6.strategy: The right recapture: it opens the d-file for the queen and the diagonal for the c8-bishop, the only compensation Black has for the pawn. The doubled pawns are the price, and Black has to play for activity.

1.Nf3 f5 2.d4.strategy: Takes the centre and transposes to the Dutch Defence with the knight already on f3, where it covers e5 and supports the d-pawn. Black keeps the claim on e4 and plays for an attack on White's kingside, at the price of a loosened kingside of his own. The game is unbalanced, with chances for both sides.

1.Nf3 f5 2.g3.strategy: Prepares Bg2 and castling while the centre pawns stay flexible: White does not yet commit to d4 or c4. The bishop looks at e4 and d5 once the knight moves. The game stays quiet and solid, at the price of leaving Black's f5 claim on e4 unchallenged for now.

1.Nf3 f5 2.c4.name: English Opening: Anglo-Dutch Defence
1.Nf3 f5 2.c4.strategy: Controls d5 and prepares Nc3 and a g3 fianchetto, a flexible set-up that can still switch to d4 later. If Black builds a wall of pawns on f5, e6 and d5, the c4-pawn presses on d5 at once. The centre is not occupied, so Black has time to set up as he likes.

1.Nf3 f5 2.e4.name: Zukertort Opening: Lisitsin Gambit
1.Nf3 f5 2.e4.background: Named after Georgy Lisitsin, who played it against Nikolai Riumin in the first round of the 1931 USSR Championship in Moscow and against Mikhail Botvinnik at the Leningrad Masters of 1933. Edward Winter gives earlier games with the same moves, the oldest being Alfred Emil Wolf against Max Weiss, played in Vienna on 12 May 1923. The Oxford Companion to Chess calls the gambit “enterprising and probably sound”.
1.Nf3 f5 2.e4.strategy: Offers the e-pawn to open lines against Black's loosened kingside. After 2...fxe4 3.Ng5 the knight attacks the pawn on e4 and is hard to chase away, so White plays for quick development and the initiative. The price is a pawn and two moves with the same piece.

1.Nf3 f5 2.b3.name: Nimzowitsch–Larsen Attack: Dutch Variation
1.Nf3 f5 2.b3.strategy: Prepares Bb2 to eye the long diagonal towards g7 and keeps White's set-up flexible. It is sound but slower than more direct moves, and Black builds the usual Dutch structure without being challenged.

1.Nf3 f5 2.d3.strategy: Prepares e4 a move later than the 2.e4 gambit, so that the d-pawn can recapture if Black takes there, and frees the c1-bishop. It is sound but slow, and Black can build the usual Dutch structure undisturbed.

1.Nf3 f5 2.e3.strategy: Opens the f1-bishop and supports a later d4, a solid set-up against the Dutch. It is sound but passive: the e3-pawn closes the c1-bishop's kingside diagonal, so that bishop usually needs b3 and Bb2, and Black develops freely.

1.Nf3 f5 2.Nc3.strategy: Develops the second knight and watches e4 and d5, keeping both d4 and e4 possible without committing a pawn. It is sound, but it blocks the c-pawn, and the plain 2.d4 reaches the same ideas with more choice.

1.Nf3 f5 2.a3.strategy: A waiting move that prepares b4 but does nothing about the centre or development. Black develops freely while White has spent a tempo on a rook-pawn move.

1.Nf3 f5 2.a4.strategy: A slow rook-pawn move that neither develops a piece nor fights for the centre. It weakens b4 and gives Black time to develop with a free hand.

1.Nf3 f5 2.b4.strategy: Grabs queenside space and prepares Bb2 on the long diagonal, but the b4-pawn needs defending against ...e6 and ...Bxb4, and the centre is left to Black. Little is gained for the tempo and the queenside is stretched.

1.Nf3 f5 2.c3.strategy: A slow preparation for d4 that takes c3 from the b1-knight and does nothing to contest e4. Black simply develops and keeps e4 under control.

1.Nf3 f5 2.h3.strategy: Prepares g4 to undermine the f5-pawn, but the plan costs time and loosens the kingside where White's king usually castles. Black simply develops.

1.Nf3 f5 2.h4.strategy: Spends a tempo on a flank pawn that does nothing for the centre or development. It weakens g4 and the kingside, and Black develops at leisure.

1.Nf3 f5 2.Na3.strategy: A rim knight that eyes c4 or b5 but covers nothing in the centre and shuts in the a-pawn. Black develops naturally.

1.Nf3 f5 2.Rg1.strategy: Prepares g4 against the f5-pawn, but White gives up the right to castle kingside and spends a tempo on the rook instead of developing. Black simply develops.

1.Nf3 f5 2.Ng5.strategy: Moves the developed knight again and invites ...h6, or ...e5 opening the queen's diagonal to g5, with a gain of time. The knight must soon return to f3 or go to the rim on h3, while Black builds the centre.

1.Nf3 f5 2.Nh4.strategy: Attacks the undefended f5-pawn, but 2...e6 defends it and opens the queen's diagonal to h4, so the knight must go back to f3 or be propped up with g3. Either way White has spent extra moves on one piece while Black develops.

1.Nf3 f5 2.Ne5.strategy: Puts the knight on a central square, but 2...d6 drives it away with a gain of time. It must retreat to f3, d3 or c4, a third move with the same piece, while Black develops.

1.Nf3 f5 2.Nd4.strategy: Attacks the undefended f5-pawn, but 2...e6 defends it at no cost, and the knight then becomes a target for ...c5. White has used two moves on the same piece and Black gains time.

1.Nf3 f5 2.Ng1.strategy: Retreats the knight to its start square and so undoes the first move. Black has ...f5 for free and builds the centre at once against an undeveloped position.

1.Nf3 f5 2.g4.strategy: Offers a pawn, but 2...fxg4 attacks the f3-knight, which has to move, and White has no lasting compensation for the pawn. The kingside is loosened for good and no new piece comes into play.

1.Nf3 f5 2.g3 Nf6.strategy: Develops the knight to its natural square, where it watches e4 and h5, and commits to no pawn set-up yet. Black keeps every Dutch structure open and decides later how to guard f5. The cost is that f5 stays unguarded for now, so a knight jump to h4 has to be kept in mind.

1.Nf3 f5 2.g3 e6.strategy: Guards f5 with a pawn and frees the f8-bishop, so castling comes quickly. Black gets a solid, flexible Dutch set-up that keeps the grip on e4. The price is the c8-bishop, which stays shut in behind the e6-pawn and needs time to find a role.

1.Nf3 f5 2.g3 g6.strategy: Guards f5 and h5 and prepares ...Bg7 on the long diagonal, a fianchetto that fits the Dutch and brings quick castling. The cost is the e6 square: with the f- and g-pawns advanced, it loses its last pawn cover once ...d6 is played, and White's knights can aim at it.

1.Nf3 f5 2.g3 d5.strategy: Claims e4 and c4 and opens the c8-bishop so that it guards f5, heading for a Stonewall set-up. The centre is fixed before the pieces are out, and a later ...e6 shuts that bishop in again.

1.Nf3 f5 2.g3 d6.strategy: Opens the c8-bishop to guard f5 and keeps ...e5 or a fianchetto available. It is flexible but slow: no piece is developed, so White can build the centre while Black is still choosing a set-up.

1.Nf3 f5 2.g3 c5.strategy: Claims d4 and queenside space for a Sicilian-style set-up. It does nothing for the f5-pawn, which still needs a guard against Nh4, and it develops no piece.

1.Nf3 f5 2.g3 c6.strategy: Prepares ...d5 with the c-pawn behind it, the usual Stonewall formation. It develops nothing and leaves f5 unguarded, so 3.Nh4 already calls for an answer.

1.Nf3 f5 2.g3 Nc6.strategy: Develops a piece at once and eyes d4 and e5. The knight takes the square of the c-pawn, so the Stonewall set-up with ...c6 is gone, and f5 stays unguarded.

1.Nf3 f5 2.g3 b6.strategy: Prepares ...Bb7, which opposes White's coming Bg2 on the long diagonal and adds a guard to e4. It develops no piece yet and leaves f5 unguarded against Nh4.

1.Nf3 f5 2.g3 Na6.strategy: Puts the knight on the rim, where it eyes b4 and c5 but stands far from the centre and blocks the a-pawn. It costs a tempo for little, and f5 stays unguarded.

1.Nf3 f5 2.g3 Nh6.strategy: Heads for f7 by way of the rim, a slow route for a knight that could reach f6 in one move. Once the c1-bishop is free, Bxh6 gxh6 would leave Black with doubled, isolated h-pawns, so the knight soon needs another move.

1.Nf3 f5 2.g3 a6.strategy: A tempo spent on a flank move with no role yet, at best preparing ...b5. It does not guard f5, so 3.Nh4 already calls for an answer.

1.Nf3 f5 2.g3 a5.strategy: Stops b4 and gains space for ...a4, but it weakens b5 and develops nothing. The f5-pawn also stays unguarded against Nh4.

1.Nf3 f5 2.g3 b5.strategy: Overextends the queenside before a single piece is out. The pawn no longer guards a6 and c6 and can be challenged by a4, and f5 stays unguarded.

1.Nf3 f5 2.g3 h6.strategy: Takes g5 away from White's pieces, but it is slow, develops nothing and leaves f5 unguarded against Nh4.

1.Nf3 f5 2.g3 h5.strategy: Gains space and prepares …h4, but the g3-pawn and the f3-knight both cover h4, so the push only drops a pawn. Meanwhile 3.Nh4 attacks the unguarded f5-pawn, so Black must answer it first.

1.Nf3 f5 2.g3 Kf7.strategy: Gives up castling for nothing and puts the king on f7, where 3.Ng5+ already checks it. The king needs further moves to reach safety.

1.Nf3 f5 2.g3 e5.strategy: Puts a second pawn forward, but nothing guards e5, so 3.Nxe5 simply wins it and Black has nothing to show for it.

1.Nf3 f5 2.g3 g5.strategy: Offers the g-pawn for nothing: 3.Nxg5 wins it, since nothing guards g5, and …h6 only chases the knight back to f3. The pawn is gone and the kingside is loosened for good.

1.Nf3 f5 2.g3 f4.strategy: Attacks g3 but simply loses a pawn: 3.gxf4 wins it, and White's doubled f-pawns are no compensation for Black, who has developed nothing.

1.Nf3 f5 2.c4 Nf6.background: The same position arises from 1.c4 f5 2.Nf3 Nf6. After 1.c4 f5, 2.d4 leads to a Dutch Defence; after White's other choices, 2.Nc3, 2.Nf3 and 2.g3, Black usually plays ...Nf6.
1.Nf3 f5 2.c4 Nf6.strategy: The natural developing move: the knight joins the f-pawn in controlling e4 and also watches d5, while Black commits to no pawn structure yet. That flexibility is the strength, and the cost is that White decides whether the game stays a quiet English or grows into a Dutch Defence.

1.Nf3 f5 2.c4 e6.strategy: Frees the f8-bishop and builds a solid, compact set-up in front of the king. The price is a c8-bishop hemmed in behind the e6-pawn and, once ...d5 is played, an e5 square that no Black pawn can cover. Black trades some activity for safety and a closed game.

1.Nf3 f5 2.c4 g6.strategy: Prepares to fianchetto the kingside bishop on the long diagonal, where it eyes White's centre and queenside. The price is a looser kingside, since the f- and g-pawns have both left their starting squares, and the king must be tucked away with care.

1.Nf3 f5 2.c4 Nc6.strategy: Develops with pressure on d4 and e5 and prepares ...e5, but the knight takes c6 from the c-pawn, so a Stonewall with ...c6 is gone, and it does nothing to control e4. A later d4-d5 can drive it away.

1.Nf3 f5 2.c4 d6.strategy: Prepares ...e5 and opens the c8-bishop's diagonal and the d7-square for the knight, but develops no piece and commits the pawn before Black knows which set-up to choose. It can wait until the knight and the e- or g-pawn have fixed the plan.

1.Nf3 f5 2.c4 c6.strategy: Prepares ...d5, backed by the c-pawn, for a Stonewall set-up. It develops no piece and takes c6 from the b8-knight, which then has to go to d7 or a6, while White develops freely.

1.Nf3 f5 2.c4 b6.strategy: Prepares ...Bb7, which joins the f-pawn in controlling e4 from the long diagonal. It is slow and develops no piece, and White can oppose the bishop on the same diagonal or take the centre.

1.Nf3 f5 2.c4 c5.strategy: Controls d4 but develops nothing, and 3.d4 cxd4 4.Nxd4 opens the centre while Black's pieces are still at home, the knight on d4 already attacking the f5-pawn. White can also simply develop.

1.Nf3 f5 2.c4 d5.strategy: Challenges the centre at once, but 3.cxd5 makes Black spend time regaining the pawn, and 3...Qxd5 is met by 4.Nc3 with tempo. Together with ...f5, the move leaves e5 and e6 without pawn cover.

1.Nf3 f5 2.c4 Na6.strategy: Puts the knight on the rim, where its only forward squares are b4 and c5, far from e4 and d5, the squares Black needs to contest. It needs another move to become active.

1.Nf3 f5 2.c4 Nh6.strategy: A rim knight that guards f5 but stands far from the centre and does nothing for e4 or d5. Once White opens the c1-bishop's diagonal, the bishop eyes h6, and Bxh6 gxh6 would leave Black with doubled, isolated h-pawns.

1.Nf3 f5 2.c4 a6.strategy: Prepares ...b5 against the c4-pawn but develops nothing and does not help control e4, so White can take the centre at leisure.

1.Nf3 f5 2.c4 a5.strategy: Stops b4 and gains queenside space, but develops nothing and leaves the centre to White.

1.Nf3 f5 2.c4 h6.strategy: A slow move that prepares ...g5 and stops Bg5 once the d-pawn has moved, but develops nothing and weakens g6.

1.Nf3 f5 2.c4 h5.strategy: Gains kingside space but develops nothing, and with the f-pawn already gone from f7 it leaves g5 and g6 without pawn cover for good.

1.Nf3 f5 2.c4 f4.strategy: Gains space against e3 and g3, but no piece supports the pawn: 3.d4 opens the c1-bishop's diagonal against it, and ...g5 to hold it allows Nxg5. White, ahead in development, can also break it up with a pawn move.

1.Nf3 f5 2.c4 b5.strategy: Gives away a pawn: 3.cxb5 takes it, and with no piece developed Black cannot use the opened lines, so White simply stays a pawn up.

1.Nf3 f5 2.c4 Kf7.strategy: Gives up the right to castle for good and develops nothing. On f7 the king is open to knight checks from g5 and e5, as in 3.e4 fxe4 4.Ng5+, which drives it on and regains the pawn.

1.Nf3 f5 2.c4 e5.strategy: Leaves the pawn unguarded: 3.Nxe5 wins it at once, and a queen move afterwards gains time against the knight but not the pawn back.

1.Nf3 f5 2.c4 g5.strategy: Loses a pawn at once: 3.Nxg5 takes the unguarded pawn and eyes h7 and e6, while the advance has weakened the kingside for nothing.

1.Nf3 f5 2.d3 Nf6.strategy: The natural developing move: the knight takes control of e4, the square White's last move prepared to occupy, so e4 can no longer be a free advance. Black keeps the Dutch set-up flexible and White has to find a plan.

1.Nf3 f5 2.c4 d6 3.e4.name: English Opening: Anglo-Dutch Variation, Chabanon Gambit
1.Nf3 f5 2.c4 d6 3.e4.strategy: A pawn offer that opens lines for the pieces at once. Black can take the pawn and defend it without trouble, so White has to prove that activity and development are worth a pawn.

1.Nf3 f5 2.d3 Nf6 3.e4.name: Zukertort Opening: Lisitsyn Gambit Deferred
1.Nf3 f5 2.d3 Nf6 3.e4.strategy: Sacrifices the e-pawn after d3 has prepared it, hoping for open lines and quick development against Black's king. If Black takes and keeps the pawn, White has to show that the initiative is worth it; it is a speculative try, not a plan with a clear return.

1.Nf3 f6 2.e4 Nh6.strategy: Puts the knight on the rim because f6 is taken by its own pawn. White's d-pawn opens the queen's bishop against the knight at once, and Bxh6 would wreck Black's kingside pawns, so Black loses time before the position is even equal.

1.Nf3 f6 2.e4 Nh6 3.d4.strategy: Takes a second central pawn and opens the queen's bishop against the knight on h6: Bxh6 gxh6 would double Black's pawns. White builds the centre with tempo while Black's knight has to retreat.

1.Nf3 f6 2.e4 Nh6 3.d4 Nf7.name: Zukertort Opening: Arctic Defence, Drunken Knight Variation
1.Nf3 f6 2.e4 Nh6 3.d4 Nf7.strategy: The knight retreats to f7, where it guards e5 and d6 and supports a central ...e5 break. Black has spent three moves on a pawn move and a knight round trip, so White has the centre and the lead in space; the game is playable but uphill.

1.Nf3 Na6 2.e4 c5.strategy: Fights for d4 at once and answers White's centre pawn with a pawn of its own. The knight stays awkwardly on the rim, but it can reroute towards c7, where it supports a later central break. Black accepts slightly slower development for a sound, flexible structure.

1.Nf3 Na6 2.e4 Nh6.name: Zukertort Opening: Drunken Cavalry Variation
1.Nf3 Na6 2.e4 Nh6.strategy: Puts a second knight on the rim without touching the centre. The h6-knight finds f5 covered by the e-pawn, and the a6-knight stands on the f1-bishop's diagonal, where Bxa6 would double Black's pawns. White builds a broad centre at leisure.

1.Nf3 Nh6 2.d4 g6.strategy: Prepares a fianchetto for the king's bishop and gives the rim knight a base, but White can trade a bishop for it at once. Playable and solid, yet passive: White has the central pawn and more space, and Black has to play for counterplay.
